title: foldPrimeBound j is Prime
content: A one-liner using `Nat.nth_mem_of_infinite Nat.infinite_setOf_prime j`. The argument: `foldPrimeBound j = Nat.nth Nat.Prime j` is the j-th element of the set `{n | Nat.Prime n}`, and `Nat.nth_mem_of_infinite` says the n-th element of an infinite set satisfies the defining predicate. The hypothesis `Nat.infinite_setOf_prime` is Euclid's theorem in Mathlib. This unlocks the key property used throughout: foldPrimeBound j has a unique prime factorization consisting of just itself.
mathContext: Since $\text{foldPrimeBound}(j) = \text{Nat.nth Nat.Prime } j$ is defined as the $j$-th member of $\{n \mid \text{Nat.Prime}(n)\}$, membership gives primality directly. The infinitude of primes (Euclid, ~300 BC) is the enabling hypothesis.

title: Lower Bound on Fold Level: j-th Prime Needs ≥ j Folds
content: The proof follows a clean diagonal argument. Suppose foldPrimeBound j is k-fold constructible with k < j. Then IsSmooth (foldPrimeBound k) (foldPrimeBound j) holds, meaning every prime factor of foldPrimeBound j is ≤ foldPrimeBound k. But foldPrimeBound j is prime (nth_prime_is_prime) and divides itself (dvd_refl), so the smoothness condition gives foldPrimeBound j ≤ foldPrimeBound k. Meanwhile, since k < j and foldPrimeBound is strictly monotone (Nat.nth_strictMono on the infinite set of primes), we have foldPrimeBound k < foldPrimeBound j. Contradiction by linarith.
mathContext: The key chain: (1) $p_j$ is prime $\Rightarrow$ $p_j$ divides itself $\Rightarrow$ smoothness gives $p_j \leq p_k$. (2) $k < j$ and strict monotonicity give $p_k < p_j$. These contradict. The argument is essentially the statement that a prime cannot be bounded by a smaller prime.

title: Upper Bound on Fold Level: j-th Prime Needs ≤ j Folds (Exact Level)
content: To show foldPrimeBound j is j-fold constructible, we need IsSmooth (foldPrimeBound j) (foldPrimeBound j). Positivity follows from primality (primes are positive). For the smoothness condition: given any prime q dividing foldPrimeBound j, since foldPrimeBound j is prime (nth_prime_is_prime), its only divisors are 1 and itself. Since q is prime, q ≠ 1, so q = foldPrimeBound j, hence q ≤ foldPrimeBound j. The `eq_one_or_self_of_dvd` lemma from Mathlib handles the case split cleanly. Combined with the lower bound theorem, `prime_exact_fold_level` gives EXACTLY j folds for j ≥ 2.
mathContext: IsSmooth$(p_j, p_j)$: the only prime dividing $p_j$ is $p_j$ itself (by primality), and $p_j \leq p_j$. Together with `nth_prime_not_constructible_below`, this gives: $\text{min\_folds}(p_j) = j$ for $j \geq 2$.

title: Main Theorem: Algebraic Completeness of Multi-fold Origami
content: The main theorem is a one-liner wrapping `eventually_constructible` from AngleTrisectionOQ05OQ01. The proof there takes k = d as the witness: all prime factors q of d satisfy q ≤ d (since q divides d), and Nat.add_two_le_nth_prime gives foldPrimeBound(d) = p_d ≥ d+2 > d, so all prime factors of d lie below the prime bound, making d a p_d-smooth number. The completeness result shows the multi-fold hierarchy is not just a proper subset of algebra — it covers all of it.
mathContext: Answer to OQ02: YES, multi-fold origami is algebraically complete. $\forall d > 0, \exists k \geq 1, \text{IsKFoldConstructible}(d, k)$. Witness: $k = d$. Proof: $q \mid d \Rightarrow q \leq d < d+2 \leq p_d = \text{foldPrimeBound}(d)$.

title: Infinite Strict Hierarchy: No Finite Fold Level Suffices
content: Proves that for any bound K, the prime p_{K+1} is a degree requiring > K folds. The proof: take d = foldPrimeBound (K+1). For k = 0: not constructible since k ≥ 1 is required. For k ≥ 1 with k ≤ K: k < K+1, so by nth_prime_not_constructible_below, foldPrimeBound(K+1) is not k-fold constructible. This shows the strictly increasing chain 1-fold ⊊ 2-fold ⊊ 3-fold ⊊ ··· never stabilizes.
mathContext: The strict chain $\text{KFold}(1) \subsetneq \text{KFold}(2) \subsetneq \text{KFold}(3) \subsetneq \cdots$ is infinite: for each level $K$, the prime $p_{K+1}$ falls outside all levels up to $K$. Equivalently: $\sup_d \text{min\_folds}(d) = \infty$ (the minimum fold level function is unbounded).
